title: Japanese Scientists Create 'Super HGF' That Could Reverse Age-Related Muscle Loss
excerpt: Researchers at Kyushu University found that a sulfur-based compound called LASSS can supercharge a key muscle-repair protein, more than doubling its effectiveness in lab tests and offering a potential new path to treating sarcopenia.
body:
• A team at Kyushu University discovered that lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS) can enhance the muscle-repair protein HGF, creating a form they call "Super HGF" with more than double the normal binding strength.
  • Aging causes chemical changes (nitration) to HGF that block its ability to activate muscle stem cells — LASSS both prevents this damage and structurally improves the protein.
  • In mouse models of muscle atrophy, LASSS pretreatment significantly reduced protein nitration, confirming the compound works in living tissue.
  • The findings, published in Scientific Reports on July 24, could lead to therapies for sarcopenia, prolonged bed rest recovery, and muscle loss in companion animals.

A sulfur-based compound can protect and dramatically enhance a protein critical to repairing damaged muscle, according to a study published July 24 in Scientific Reports. The discovery by researchers at Kyushu University in Fukuoka, Japan, opens a potential new front in the fight against sarcopenia — the gradual loss of muscle mass and strength that affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide as they age.

The research team, led by Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi at Kyushu University's Faculty of Agriculture, found that a molecule called lipoic acid trisulfide (LASSS) doesn't just shield the muscle-repair protein hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) from age-related damage — it structurally transforms it into a supercharged version the team has dubbed "Super HGF."

How Aging Breaks Muscle Repair

In healthy muscle, HGF functions as a wake-up signal. It sits quietly in the tissue surrounding muscle fibres until injury or mechanical stress triggers its release. HGF then binds to c-met receptors on satellite cells — the resident stem cells of skeletal muscle — prompting them to activate, multiply, and repair damage.

But aging disrupts this process through a chemical reaction called nitration. A nitro group attaches to two specific sites on the HGF protein — Y198 and Y250 — which happen to be exactly where HGF connects with its receptor. The result, as the researchers describe it, is like a rusted key that no longer fits its lock.

"HGF is not necessarily missing as we age. Rather, it can be chemically altered after it is made. That led us to wonder whether a compound with strong antioxidant capacity might protect HGF, either by preventing nitration or by compensating for the functional loss it causes."

— Professor Ryuichi Tatsumi, Kyushu University

From Protection to Enhancement

Tatsumi's team tested two trisulfide compounds — molecules containing three sulfur atoms linked in sequence — known for powerful antioxidant properties: glutathione trisulfide (GSSSG) and LASSS. Both initially suppressed HGF nitration at the critical Y198 and Y250 sites, but neither fully restored the protein's receptor-binding ability.

The breakthrough came when the researchers increased the molar ratio of HGF to trisulfide from 1:4,000 to 1:8,000. At the higher concentration, LASSS didn't just protect HGF — it more than doubled its binding affinity for the c-met receptor compared with untreated HGF, while also making the protein more resistant to nitration damage. GSSSG showed no such enhancement, making LASSS's effect uniquely potent.

"This exceeded our expectations," Tatsumi said, according to News-Medical.net. "We knew trisulfides had diverse biological functions, but we never expected that simply mixing HGF with LASSS would produce such a striking effect. What this tells us is that LASSS does more than simply neutralize reactive molecules. It may interact directly with HGF and induce a subtle structural change, creating an enhanced 'Super HGF' form that binds c-met more strongly and resists nitration."

From Test Tube to Living Tissue

To test whether these lab results held up in a biological system, the team used a mouse model of muscle atrophy induced by tail suspension — a standard method for simulating disuse-related muscle loss. Mice pretreated with LASSS showed significantly reduced nitration of HGF compared with untreated animals. GSSSG again provided no protective benefit, confirming that LASSS's advantages carried over from the laboratory to living tissue.

The study was published in Scientific Reports (DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-60835-w), a peer-reviewed Nature Portfolio journal. Further studies in aging animal models will be needed to confirm LASSS's long-term effectiveness and safety before any human trials can begin.

Why It Matters for India's Aging Population

Sarcopenia is a growing global concern, and India is no exception. The country's population aged 60 and above is projected to reach 347 million by 2050, according to UN estimates. Muscle wasting already contributes to falls, fractures, and loss of independence among older Indians, with limited treatment options beyond exercise and nutrition — interventions that are often insufficient on their own.

A targeted pharmaceutical therapy for age-related muscle loss could have outsized benefits in countries like India, where geriatric care infrastructure is still developing and where maintaining physical independence is closely tied to family well-being and caregiving dynamics in multigenerational households.

What's Next

The Kyushu University team believes LASSS's effects on HGF are likely to apply broadly across species, including companion animals like cats and dogs. The immediate priority is confirming these results in aging animal models before exploring clinical applications. If the compound's enhancement of HGF proves safe and durable in vivo, it could lead to new treatments not only for age-related sarcopenia but also for muscle loss caused by prolonged hospitalisation, bed rest, or disuse.

The research represents one of several recent advances in understanding how aging impairs muscle repair at the molecular level. Unlike approaches that try to replace lost muscle tissue or boost stem cell numbers, the Kyushu team's strategy targets the signalling pathway itself — potentially fixing the broken communication line between damaged muscle and the cells meant to repair it.
